\section[\texorpdfstring{\ja{まちかど} (machikado)}{まちかど (machikado)}]{\ja{まちかど} (machikado) — a street corner}

\label{lesson:JA-C82-machikado}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Japanese for between, then the Japanese for a region.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ja{まちかど}}
\textbf{\ja{まちかど}} — \emph{machikado} — \textquotedblleft{}a street corner\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ja{まちかど}} (\emph{machikado}) is a native compound, inherited rather than borrowed: \emph{machi}, \textquotedblleft{}town, street\textquotedblright{}, and \emph{kado}, \textquotedblleft{}corner\textquotedblright{}, both kun'yomi of its kanji (JMdict, KANJIDIC2).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for this chapter.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright

  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{machikado}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} say \emph{machikado}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Japanese for between, then the Japanese for a region, then say \emph{machikado} again
\end{itemize}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\ja{しない} (shinai)}{しない (shinai)}]{\ja{しない} (shinai) — within the city}

\label{lesson:JA-C82-shinai}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Japanese for a region, then the Japanese for a street corner.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ja{しない}}
\textbf{\ja{しない}} — \emph{shinai} — \textquotedblleft{}within the city\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ja{しない}} (\emph{shinai}) is Sino-Japanese (kango): two Chinese characters read with their on'yomi, readings borrowed from Chinese. They are \emph{shi}, \textquotedblleft{}market, city\textquotedblright{} (Middle Chinese \emph{dzyiX}) and \emph{nai}, \textquotedblleft{}inside\textquotedblright{} (\emph{nwojH}) (Unihan, KANJIDIC2; Middle Chinese in Baxter's transcription).
\end{cousinweb}

\end{grammarlens}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\ja{はんたいがわ} (hantaigawa)}{はんたいがわ (hantaigawa)}]{\ja{はんたいがわ} (hantaigawa) — the opposite side}

\label{lesson:JA-C82-hantaigawa}

Before the new one: say the Japanese for within the city, then the Japanese for the suburbs.

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ja{はんたいがわ}}
\textbf{\ja{はんたいがわ}} — \emph{hantaigawa} — \textquotedblleft{}the opposite side\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ja{はんたいがわ}} (\emph{hantaigawa}) mixes the two layers: \emph{hantai}, \textquotedblleft{}opposite\textquotedblright{}, borrowed from Chinese, \emph{han}, \textquotedblleft{}reverse, opposite\textquotedblright{} (Middle Chinese \emph{pjonX}), and \emph{tai}, \textquotedblleft{}facing\textquotedblright{} (Middle Chinese \emph{twojH}), with native \emph{kawa}, \textquotedblleft{}side\textquotedblright{}, voiced to \emph{gawa} (JMdict; Unihan, KANJIDIC2).
\end{cousinweb}
